brief.head: Tyrannies leak
brief.text: Authoritarian regimes are full of obe­di­ent peo­ple who hate the ruler, Ajay Shah said, which makes them rich ground for human in­tel­li­gence, or HUMINT. {015-C01}

brief.head: Wanted: a Mahalanobis
brief.text: Excellence comes from ec­cen­tric, con­fi­dent, crazy, cre­ative founders, Ajay Shah ar­gued, not from gov­ern­ment bu­reau­cra­cies. He is scep­ti­cal of calls for more pub­lic-sector uni­ver­si­ties. {015-C07}

brief.head: Not button-pushing
brief.text: Too many peo­ple treat sta­tis­tics as throw­ing data into a soft­ware pack­age and read­ing off an­swers, Ajay Shah warned. Intuition and com­mon sense, he said, must be pre­served. {015-C04}

brief.head: On a wing and a prayer
brief.text: Ajay Shah traced the phrase to Second World War bombers with their en­gines shot out, glid­ing home on just a wing and pray­ing to reach in time. {015-J18}

brief.head: High modernism
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s term for a two-part be­lief: sci­en­tists and en­gi­neers know what to do, and that en­ti­tles them to co­erce ev­ery­one else. It “works pretty badly”, he said. {015-C09}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.who: Ajay Shah, on starting a PhD having never studied probability or statistics

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on CR Rao and his world
lead.head: Counting on Calcutta

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma in Episode 15

body: Late in the Second World War, the Allies needed to know how many heavy tanks Germany made each month. Spies, the peo­ple “who knew the girl­friend of some brigadier”, said about 1,500. Statisticians, read­ing the se­rial num­bers on de­stroyed tanks, said about 200.
After the war, Germany’s own pro­duc­tion records showed the statis­ti­cians were right. “The moral of the story,” Amit Varma said, “is brigadiers lie to their girl­friends.” {015-J01}
“Or that tanks don’t lie,” Ajay Shah replied.
The tanks were only a warm-up for Shah’s trib­ute to his hero, the statis­ti­cian CR Rao, who had died days be­fore they recorded.
## A hero made in Calcutta

Rao, born in 1920, came from Andhra Pradesh to Calcutta as an or­di­nary stu­dent at PC Mahalanobis’s Indian Statistical Institute. It was be­fore in­de­pen­dence, with no gov­ern­ment money; Mahalanobis often paid from his own pocket.

Cut off from the European main­stream, Rao pro­duced two of what Shah counts among the great­est re­sults of 20th-century sta­tis­tics: the Cramér-Rao lower bound, in 1943, and the Rao-Blackwell the­o­rem.

The first sets a limit on how good an es­ti­ma­tor, a for­mula for in­fer­ring an un­known, can ever be. “You can run and run and build bet­ter and bet­ter es­ti­ma­tors,” Shah said, “but you can’t cross the Cramér-Rao lower bound.” {015-C02}

Shah sees Rao as the prod­uct of an Indian ecosys­tem, more like the chess player Anand than Ramanujan, and so the great­est achieve­ment of the Bengal Renaissance. Varma hap­pily agreed: “You know the whole world is Bengali.”

Rao’s name sur­vived, Shah said, thanks to the statis­ti­cian Ronald Fisher, who vis­ited the in­sti­tute, grasped the re­sults and began call­ing them by both names. “And sud­denly for the whole world, it be­came Rao’s work.” {015-S03}
## Bullets and bombers

Varma an­swered with British planes. Returning air­craft had more bul­let holes in the fuse­lage than in the en­gine. Abraham Wald asked: where are the miss­ing bul­lets? In the planes that never came back, so the en­gine was what needed pro­tect­ing. {015-S06}
Shah named the trap sur­vivor­ship bias, then raised Varma with Allied bombers over Germany.

Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, out of reach of the guns, but from there very few bombs hit. Counting lives lost per fac­tory de­stroyed, the statis­ti­cians, a young Robert McNamara among them, chose 6,000 feet.
## A sur­vey and a plan­ner

Varma then turned to Mahalanobis, read­ing from Nikhil Menon’s *Planning Democracy*. In 1944, mea­sur­ing Bengal’s jute, the institute’s sam­ple sur­vey erred by 0.3 per cent, the government’s count by 16.6 per cent. The sur­vey cost a tenth as much. {015-C11}
Yet the man who could mea­sure a crop was, in Menon’s por­trait, a prim worka­holic who “thought he knew best in prac­ti­cally every mat­ter”. Varma called him a ge­nius “trapped by his own ge­nius”.

The plan­ning state reached far. In 1956, Varma said, a bill set out to li­cense India’s es­ti­mated 75 lakh sad­hus, and President Rajendra Prasad’s speech to them was, in Varma’s read­ing, a pitch for the Five-Year Plan.

There was colour, too. JBS Haldane moved to India, he said, be­cause he didn’t want to wear socks any­more. Chintaman Deshmukh, whose sanc­tion of funds kept the in­sti­tute alive, pro­posed by in­scrib­ing Sanskrit shlokas on a eu­ca­lyp­tus tree.
Shah’s part­ing pick was David Salsburg’s *The Lady Tasting Tea*, a fun book, he said, even for those who have never done any sta­tis­tics.

second.label: The German tank problem
second.head: Spies, outnumbered
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how statisticians outguessed the spies about German tanks

pic.caption: A Tiger I tank on display at Bovington Tank Museum in 2008

body: Late in the Second World War, the Allies wanted to know whether Germany’s new heavy tanks were “a few ar­ti­sanal demo parts” or were being made at scale. The me­thod­i­cal Germans, Ajay Shah said, num­bered every tank in se­quence.
So if de­stroyed tanks bore the num­bers 24, 74 and 90, do not con­clude that there are only 90. Take the av­er­age gap be­tween the num­bers and add it to the high­est. {#gap}

The spies put pro­duc­tion at about 1,500 tanks a month; the statis­ti­cians, at about 200. After the war, German pro­duc­tion records set­tled the de­bate: “the statis­ti­cians were right and the humint was wrong”. {015-S01}

quote.text: Just imag­ine this would have been harder if they had ran­dom­ized every num­ber.

third.head: Code that made Rao smile

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the package named after CR Rao

body: Ajay Shah’s clos­est brush with his hero came through soft­ware. His col­league Sourish Das, at the Chennai Mathematical Institute, leads a sta­tis­tics pack­age writ­ten in Julia, a pro­gram­ming lan­guage Shah loves.
It of­fers one way to call many kinds of es­ti­ma­tors, from lin­ear re­gres­sion to ran­dom forests, in ei­ther fre­quen­tist or Bayesian form. {015-R08}
When the team de­bated names, Das pro­posed CRRao.jl as “a com­mit­ment de­vice”, a way to kick him­self into doing it well. Amit Varma ap­proved: “We should have called the show CR Rao.” {015-J06}
Then Rao’s daugh­ter wrote to say she had shown him the pack­age, and he had smiled. “That is the clos­est that I ever came to the great­ness that is CR Rao,” Shah said. {015-S05}

box.text: CR Rao was born in 1920 and came to Calcutta from Andhra Pradesh as a young man. Ajay Shah calls him one of the great fig­ures of the 20th cen­tury, and the great­est achieve­ment of the Bengal Renaissance. {#greatfigure}

sections.label: The hero
sections.head: An Anand, not a Ramanujan
sections.caption: CR Rao and two kinds of Indian genius
body: Ajay Shah began his PhD with­out ever hav­ing stud­ied prob­a­bil­ity or sta­tis­tics, so he was placed in a fourth-year un­der­grad­u­ate econo­met­rics class taught by Dennis Aigner. Aigner’s open­ing “he­li­copter tour” of all sta­tis­tics swept him away.

As Aigner made one es­ti­ma­tor bet­ter, and then bet­ter again, Shah put up his hand: surely there had to be a the­o­ret­i­cal limit. Aigner replied that an Indian had asked ex­actly that ques­tion, and an­swered it. {015-S02}

The an­swer was the Cramér-Rao lower bound, which CR Rao proved in Calcutta in 1943. His sec­ond great re­sult, the Rao-Blackwell the­o­rem, is a tech­nique for mak­ing an es­ti­ma­tor one step bet­ter.
## Two kinds of ge­nius

Shah set Rao against two mod­els of Indian ge­nius. Ramanujan built him­self in iso­la­tion, but it was GH Hardy and Cambridge that made him one of the world’s great math­e­ma­ti­cians. Anand was made by an Indian chess ecosys­tem, and then nur­tured the next gen­er­a­tion.

Rao, Shah ar­gued, is the Anand story. He was no pre­co­cious child writ­ing let­ters from afar. He came to the Indian Statistical Institute as a reg­u­lar stu­dent and “ex­ploded in the world cre­ated by Mahalanobis”. {015-C06}
Amit Varma added the American Statistical Association’s praise of Rao as “a liv­ing leg­end”, whose work reached fields from eco­nom­ics and ge­net­ics to medicine. {015-J22}
~ So, “at the risk of of­fend­ing Bengalis all over the world”, Shah claimed Rao as the great­est achieve­ment of the Bengal Renaissance.

quote.text: CR Rao to me is a lit­tle more of an Anand story and not the Ramanujan story.

sections.label: The head start
sections.head: Credit given, boat missed
sections.caption: credit, founders and a missed boat
body: When work is done in India, Ajay Shah said, the global main­stream very often ig­nores it. “We see this even today in the age of the in­ter­net,” he said. It has hap­pened to him: work of his that was ahead of the main­stream went uncited while oth­ers claimed the line. {015-C08}

CR Rao’s re­sults sur­vived be­cause of Ronald Fisher, who un­der­stood them on his vis­its to ISI and began call­ing them by the joint names. Shah likened those names to a “Darwin-Wallace the­ory of evo­lu­tion”. {015-J20}
## The founder’s touch
One Rao con­vinced a gen­er­a­tion at ISI that “this is a game we can play”. The in­sti­tute was world-class, and its jour­nal, *Sankhya*, was taken by li­braries all over the world. {015-J21}
All this hap­pened be­fore in­de­pen­dence, with­out gov­ern­ment fund­ing. That, for Shah, is the les­son: ex­cel­lence comes from an ec­cen­tric founder, not from a bu­reau­cracy.

But the head start did not last. From the 1970s, the fron­tier moved to com­pu­ta­tional sta­tis­tics, where, as Shah put it, “an es­ti­ma­tor can be an al­go­rithm”. India’s statis­ti­cians kept prov­ing the­o­rems, and “didn’t turn on the dime and rein­vent them­selves”. {015-S04}
~ Amit Varma had a smaller worry: that “you and I will miss the boat on the YouTube al­go­rithm”. {015-J08}

quote.text: Having one CR Rao made a huge dif­fer­ence to a whole gen­er­a­tion of statis­ti­cians

art.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on credit, founders and a missed boat, with Amit Varma

sections.label: The survivors
sections.head: The bullets that weren’t there
sections.caption: Abraham Wald and the missing bullets
body: Around 1942, Amit Varma said, Abraham Wald was drafted into a wartime re­search group so bril­liant that some­one quipped Milton Friedman was the fourth smartest per­son in the room. Wald had no se­cu­rity clear­ance; the joke went that a sec­re­tary whisked away each sheet as soon as he fin­ished it. {015-J03}
The group was asked how to make planes that came back rid­dled with bul­lets stronger. The en­gines had fewer holes than the fuse­lage, so the ob­vi­ous plan was to strengthen the fuse­lage.
Wald asked where the miss­ing bul­lets were. If hits are spread evenly, they struck the planes that went down. “So it is the en­gine that you need to pro­tect.” {015-S06}
Varma found the same in­sight, ar­rived at by in­stinct, in the bats­man Ricky Ponting: “Most bats­men have a map of the field­ers in their head. I had a map of the gaps.” {015-J19}
## Mind the sur­vivors

Ajay Shah named it sur­vivor­ship bias. “When you see the data set, you are see­ing the sur­vivors,” he said. The ones that died along the way are in­vis­i­ble, so think about where data came from be­fore using it. {015-C03}
~ The same trap, Varma said, makes a fund’s five- or six-year record mean­ing­less: run enough ran­dom strate­gies and one will come out on top by chance.

quote.text: Where are the miss­ing bul­lets? The miss­ing bul­lets are in the planes that went down.

portraits.caption: Abraham Wald
portraits.credit: Konrad Jacobs, Erlangen, Copyright is MFO, CC BY-SA 2.0 de

sections.label: The bombers
sections.head: The arithmetic of 6,000 feet
sections.caption: how many lives it takes to kill a factory
body: Allied bombers flew from Britain to de­stroy tar­gets such as oil re­finer­ies and tank fac­to­ries, Ajay Shah said, run­ning into German fight­ers and the 88-millimetre anti-aircraft gun.
Bombs then fell under grav­ity alone, Shah said, and the error could run from one kilo­me­tre to five. {#cep}

Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, out of range of the guns. From there, though, very few bombs hit their tar­get. At 6,000 feet more crews would be shot down, but far more bombs would find the fac­tory.
## Counting the cost

The statis­ti­cians, a young Robert McNamara among them, set aside the pilots’ fear and asked an­other ques­tion. “How many lives does it take to kill a fac­tory?” Shah said. {015-C10} The an­swer was 6,000 feet.

The pi­lots were in up­roar: fly­ing that low, they said, was death. In Shah’s telling, McNamara and Curtis LeMay, the head of bomber com­mand, replied: “We love you more than life it­self, but we want fewer of you to die.” {015-S08}
~ The dam­age was checked af­ter­wards by a spot­ter plane, by local in­tel­li­gence and, Shah added, by “the brigadier’s girl­friend”. {015-J02}

quote.text: And the bru­tal an­swer turns out that you have to fly at 6,000 feet.

portraits.caption: Robert McNamara
portraits.credit: DoD photo by Oscar Porter, U.S. Army., public domain

sections.label: The professor
sections.head: The man who thought he knew
sections.caption: PC Mahalanobis, sampler and planner
body: PC Mahalanobis trained in physics, Amit Varma said. On the voy­age home he was given vol­umes of the sta­tis­tics jour­nal *Biometrika*, and by the time he landed in India, sta­tis­tics was his love.

Reading from Nikhil Menon’s *Planning Democracy*, Varma de­scribed a stern, prim worka­holic with hair slicked flat by co­conut oil, who showed af­fec­tion only to his pets: dogs, cats and cows. The rest of it, Varma told Ajay Shah, seemed to fit him. “Cows also,” Shah replied. {015-J11}
## The jute test

In 1944 the Bengal gov­ern­ment pit­ted the institute’s ran­dom sam­ple sur­vey against plot-by-plot count­ing of jute, check­ing both against of­fi­cial sales fig­ures. The count was off by 16.6 per cent, the sur­vey by 0.3 per cent. {015-S11}
Success bred cer­tainty. Milton Friedman, quoted by Varma, warned that able math­e­ma­ti­cians, “work­ing in a field of ab­so­lutes”, grow dan­ger­ous when they turn to eco­nomic plan­ning. {015-J23}
Mahalanobis made stu­dents and staff record their daily ac­tiv­i­ties in a diary. He, Varma told Shah, “would have loved Aadhaar”. {015-J12}
~ Shah saw a re­cur­ring theme: the cer­tainty of sci­ence and en­gi­neer­ing leaves many suc­cess­ful peo­ple un­pre­pared for the com­plex­i­ties of the real world.

quote.text: A man who is a ge­nius, but in a sense is also trapped by his own ge­nius into a hubris and an ar­ro­gance

For too many peo­ple, sta­tis­tics has be­come a me­chan­i­cal process where you throw some data into some soft­ware pack­age and you get some an­swers. And al­ways and al­ways it is im­por­tant to pre­serve fun­da­men­tal in­tu­ition and in­sight and com­mon sense.

p3.title: Sadhus, socks and shlokas
p3.deck: Four tales Amit Varma told, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the official who saved ISI, and his proposal
stories.head: A proposal written on bark
body: Around 1944, a se­nior gov­ern­ment of­fi­cial named Chintaman Deshmukh, later fi­nance min­is­ter, ap­proved a flow of funds to the Indian Statistical Institute. It prac­ti­cally guar­an­teed, Amit Varma said, that the in­sti­tute would sur­vive.

Varma read from Nikhil Menon’s por­trait of him in *Planning Democracy*: a prod­uct of Bombay and Cambridge who ranked first in the Indian Civil Service, re­cited Vedic shlokas for plea­sure, trans­lated Kalidasa’s *Meghaduta* from Sanskrit and quoted scrip­ture “to but­tress eco­nomic pol­icy”.
Varma had never heard of him be­fore, and got cu­ri­ous. Widowed in the early 1950s, Deshmukh had mar­ried Durgabai Deshmukh.

She had been mar­ried off as a child, at eight. {#eight} At 14, be­fore the mar­riage was con­sum­mated, she told her fa­ther she would not go through with it, and the man was lib­eral enough to let her go.

She was feisty and out­spo­ken, and peo­ple were aghast at the mar­riage: he was so­phis­ti­cated, while she would say what­ever came into her head. Varma searched hard for her au­to­bi­og­ra­phy, *Chintaman and I*, found it nei­ther on Kindle nor any­where else, and at last found a free copy on­line. {015-R06}

Its open­ing lines are the pro­posal: “Chintaman took me to a eu­ca­lyp­tus tree in his gar­den and in­scribed two Sanskrit slokas on its bark. It was a pro­posal of mar­riage. I ac­cepted and he kissed me.” {015-S14}
~ Varma asked Ajay Shah whether he had ever in­scribed shlokas into the bark of a tree. “No, no such luck,” came the an­swer. {015-J15}
stories.why: The man who saved a sta­tis­tics in­sti­tute was also a ro­man­tic, and his wife opened her au­to­bi­og­ra­phy with his pro­posal. Even peo­ple who care about sta­tis­tics and math, Varma con­cluded, have hearts.
stories.postscript: The funds came around the time Mahalanobis bested the Bengal government’s count. Whether there was a causal link, Varma said, he did not know.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Chintaman Deshmukh’s proposal

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how far the planning state reached
stories.head: Licensed to renounce
body: In the mid-1950s, Amit Varma said, India was es­ti­mated to have some 75 lakh sad­hus. {#sadhus} Many, the think­ing went, were frauds and char­la­tans. How was one to iden­tify a gen­uine sadhu? “Obviously, the gov­ern­ment has to do it.”
So in 1956 a sadhu reg­is­tra­tion bill was brought in. Anyone want­ing to be known as a sadhu would apply to the gov­ern­ment for a li­cence and join the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj.

President Rajendra Prasad then ad­dressed the gath­ered sad­hus: “It is not pos­si­ble to achieve any­thing in the other world with­out set­ting things in order in this world.” His real sub­ject, Varma said, was the Five-Year Plan. {015-S12}

~ Ajay Shah wanted to know: “Was there a cer­ti­fi­ca­tion ex­am­i­na­tion? Was there a UID?” Varma did not know, but pic­tured li­censed sad­hus with their “doc­u­men­ta­tion in trip­li­cate”. {015-J13}

quote.text: You wanna be good in that world, you gotta be good in this world. Five year plan will get you there.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on JBS Haldane, and a lesson for writers
stories.head: The case against socks
body: JBS Haldane came to work at the Indian Statistical Institute in the mid-1950s, in his six­ties. Of PC Mahalanobis, al­ways on the move, he said: “The jour­ney­ings of our di­rec­tor de­fine a novel ran­dom vec­tor.” Amit Varma con­fessed he had no idea what that meant. {015-J17}
Asked why he had left England for India, Haldane could have said he wanted a sim­ple life, free of con­ven­tion. Instead he said: “I don’t want to wear socks any­more.” {015-S13}

“Everybody im­me­di­ately gets a vibe,” Varma said. For him it is a great ex­am­ple of a writ­ing prin­ci­ple, show, don’t tell: “don’t tell some­thing in straight words, show it with some­thing.” {015-C12}
~ In pic­tures from the rest of his life, Haldane is in banyan, dhoti and py­jama, “but never a sock in sight”.
stories.why: A sin­gle con­crete de­tail can carry a whole phi­los­o­phy of life. Haldane never had to ex­plain his move in ab­stract words about sim­plic­ity or con­ven­tion; the socks said it, and ev­ery­one un­der­stood.
stories.postscript: Varma rec­om­mends Samanth Subramanian’s *A Dominant Character*, “a great book” on Haldane. {015-R05}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Haldane and his socks

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on survivorship bias, a con artist’s friend
stories.head: The tipster who can’t lose
body: Amit Varma once wrote a col­umn built on a scam. Write to a thou­sand peo­ple who bet on cricket and offer free tips on the next India–Sri Lanka match. Tell 500 of them India will win, and 500 that Sri Lanka will. {#fivehundred}
Whoever wins, 500 peo­ple now know you got it right. Split them, and do it again.
By the time the group is down to ten or twelve, they have seen you call four, five, six re­sults in a row. “They’re will­ing to pay their money.”

~ Mutual funds can work the same way, Varma said. Run a fam­ily of funds on ran­dom strate­gies, and by sheer dumb luck one will come out on top. “But it doesn’t mean that that is a cor­rect strat­egy. Perhaps it just got lucky.” {015-S07}
stories.why: A great track record means lit­tle until you know how many at­tempts failed and van­ished, and se­lec­tion can look ex­actly like skill. Ajay Shah’s name for the trap is sur­vivor­ship bias: the data shows only the sur­vivors. {015-C03}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 15. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao (Prateek Karandikar, CC BY-SA 4.0); Tiger I (Hohum, CC BY 3.0); Srinivasa Ramanujan (Konrad Jacobs, public domain); Viswanathan Anand (Wolfgang Jekel, CC BY 2.0); Ronald Fisher (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Abraham Wald (Konrad Jacobs, Erlangen, Copyright is MFO, CC BY-SA 2.0 de); Robert McNamara (DoD photo by Oscar Porter, U.S. Army., public domain); Curtis LeMay (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis (Parinitha Ravi, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: The Great Mental Models (three-volume set)
shelf.creator: Shane Parrish (Farnam Street)
shelf.why: Formal ed­u­ca­tion rarely teaches how to think about the world.

shelf.title: The Knowledge Project Podcast
shelf.creator: Shane Parrish
shelf.why: Amit calls it ‘the ex­cel­lent Knowledge Project podcast’.

shelf.title: The Lady Tasting Tea
shelf.creator: David Salsburg
shelf.why: Fun even if you have never stud­ied sta­tis­tics.

shelf.title: Planning Democracy
shelf.creator: Nikhil Menon
shelf.why: It is full of vivid por­traits and strange his­tory from India’s plan­ning era.

shelf.title: A Dominant Character
shelf.creator: Samanth Subramanian
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great book on Haldane, the sci­en­tist who spent his last years in India.

shelf.title: Chintaman and I
shelf.creator: Durgabai Deshmukh
shelf.why: He loves its open­ing lines, in which Chintaman pro­poses by carv­ing Sanskrit shlokas into a eu­ca­lyp­tus tree.

shelf.title: The Julia Programming Language
shelf.creator: Viral Shah (co-creator)
shelf.why: Ajay calls it one of the great achieve­ments of mod­ern pro­gram­ming.

shelf.title: CRRao.jl
shelf.creator: Sourish Das / XKDR Forum
shelf.why: It gives one con­sis­tent in­ter­face across many es­ti­ma­tors and is un­com­pro­mis­ingly Bayesian, re­mov­ing the extra ef­fort Bayesian com­pu­ta­tion usu­ally re­quires.

shelf.title: Doing applied statistics research in Julia
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A fol­low-up for any­one in­ter­ested in the case for doing data anal­y­sis in Julia.

shelf.title: Don’t Get Fooled by Success (2005)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn on sur­vivor­ship bias: a fund’s track record can be pure luck, so don’t read suc­cess sto­ries as proof of ge­nius when many sim­i­lar at­tempts may have failed un­seen.

shelf.title: Two great investment strategies (1998)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s older piece on in­vest­ing, a cau­tion that sto­ries of great fund man­agers are mostly sur­vivor­ship bias and that track records can mis­lead.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen, Episode 183: The Art of Narrative Nonfiction (with Samanth Subramanian)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The longer con­ver­sa­tion be­hind the Haldane sto­ries and the ‘show, don’t tell’ ex­am­ple.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything, Episode 8: Why Talent Comes in Clusters
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything, Episode 10: Why Freedom Matters
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Tamilian gentleman who took on the world
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s piece on Viswanathan Anand ris­ing with­out the Soviet school’s sys­tem­atic train­ing, like tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race, which shows how ex­tra­or­di­nary his world-championship ca­reer was.

shelf.title: Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao: A brief biography
shelf.why: For read­ers who want more on the man Ajay calls the finest prod­uct of the Bengal Renaissance.

shelf.title: The German Tank Problem explained
shelf.creator: NStatum
shelf.why: A vis­ual walk-through of the es­ti­ma­tion idea Ajay de­scribes, in which se­rial num­bers re­veal how many tanks were made.

laughs.text: After the German Tank Problem, Amit of­fers the moral: ‘The moral of the story is brigadiers lie to their girl­friends.’ Ajay adds: ‘Or that tanks don’t lie.’

Amit on Wald’s wartime group: it was so bril­liant that some­one quipped ‘Milton Friedman is the fourth smartest per­son in the room’. And be­cause Wald lacked se­cu­rity clear­ance, the joke went that a sec­re­tary took away each sheet the mo­ment he fin­ished writ­ing it.

After read­ing Nikhil Menon’s por­trait of a stern, prim Mahalanobis who showed af­fec­tion only to dogs, cats and cows, Amit tells Ajay that apart from the dogs and cows, ‘the rest of this seems to fit you’. Ajay replies: ‘Cows also.’
On Mahalanobis mak­ing staff log their daily ac­tiv­i­ties, Amit says to Ajay, the pri­vacy ad­vo­cate: ‘he would have loved Aadhaar’.

On the gov­ern­ment li­cens­ing sad­hus, Ajay asks: ‘Was there a cer­ti­fi­ca­tion ex­am­i­na­tion? Was there a UID?’ Amit trips over his words: ‘Once the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj was farmed, formed, not farmed, you could farm them’, with sadhus’ ‘doc­u­men­ta­tion in triplicate’.
Amit quotes Haldane’s line that Mahalanobis’s con­stant trav­els ‘de­fine a novel ran­dom vector’, then ad­mits: ‘I have no idea what that phrase means, but I’m sure you do.’

After the story of India miss­ing the boat on com­pu­ta­tional sta­tis­tics, Amit says: ‘We missed the boat on al­go­rithms and what I’m wor­ried about is that you and I will miss the boat on the YouTube al­go­rithm.’ He fol­lows with a pun on going viral and Viral Shah, the Julia co-creator Ajay had just men­tioned.

‘Coming back on a wing and a prayer’: Ajay calls it one of the most beau­ti­ful phrases in English and traces it to WWII bombers whose en­gines were shot out, glid­ing home on just a wing and hop­ing to make it.
Ricky Ponting on be­com­ing a great bats­man, quoted by Amit as an in­tu­itive ver­sion of Wald’s in­sight: ‘Most bats­men have a map of the field­ers in their head. I had a map of the gaps.’

Darwin and Wallace: Ajay com­pares the joint names on Rao’s the­o­rems to the ‘Darwin-Wallace the­ory of evolution’. The Royal Society gave both men credit, even though Wallace had his idea in a malaria fever dream weeks ear­lier while Darwin had been work­ing on it for decades.

Milton Friedman on Mahalanobis, quoted by Amit: able math­e­ma­ti­cians, ‘work­ing in a field of absolutes’, be­come dan­ger­ous in eco­nomic plan­ning be­cause ‘they pro­duce spe­cific and de­tailed plans in which they have con­fi­dence with­out per­haps re­al­iz­ing that eco­nomic plan­ning is not the ab­so­lute sci­ence that math­e­mat­ics is.’
